summary.text: The instrumental temperature record is the record of Earth's air and ocean temperatures built from direct measurements.
Reliable series began in some regions between 1850 and 1880, with data coming mainly from weather stations and satellites.
Its rising global surface temperature is one of many lines of evidence that human activities are causing climate change.

items.prompt: Global temperature rose before 1940, then held fairly steady until about 1970 before climbing again. What has the mid-century pause mostly been blamed on?

options.label: A run of unusually cold winters
Sulfate aerosols in the air
Fewer weather stations reporting
A dip in the Sun's brightness

items.explain: The cooling or plateau from 1940 to 1970 has been mostly attributed to sulfate aerosol.

items.prompt: From 1850–1900 to 2011–2020, which warmed more: the continents or the oceans?

options.label: The sea surface, by about double
Both warmed by the same amount
Air over land, by nearly double
Neither changed noticeably

items.explain: Land air temperatures rose about 1.59 °C while sea surface temperatures rose about 0.88 °C.

items.prompt: A skeptic argues that warming in the global record is just cities heating up around thermometers. What do the measurements suggest?

options.label: City heat explains most of the warming
City heat is corrected by ignoring land data
Cities have cooled the record overall
Uncorrected city effects likely add under 10%

items.explain: It is unlikely that uncorrected urbanisation or land-use effects raised global land warming by more than 10%, though some fast-growing regions show local signals.

items.prompt: One year runs warmer than the trend and the next runs cooler, even as the long-term line keeps rising. What can cause such ups and downs?

options.label: Natural swings such as El Niño
Thermometers being swapped each year
Satellites measuring only the poles
The record skipping alternate years

items.explain: Within the upward trend, some variability comes from natural internal swings such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation.

items.prompt: To build the global surface temperature, scientists combine sea surface and land air readings. How are the two parts weighted?

options.label: Equally, half and half
By how many people live there
By the area each covers
By how many stations each has

items.explain: Global surface temperature combines sea surface and land air temperatures, weighted by their respective areas.

items.prompt: Scientists want temperatures from 500 years ago, long before thermometers were common. What can they use?

options.label: Weather balloon launches
Tree rings and ice cores
Old satellite photographs
Ocean heat content data

items.explain: For the distant past, proxy data from tree rings, corals and ice cores can stand in for direct measurements.

paragraphs.heading: What is measured
paragraphs.text: The instrumental temperature record is the record of Earth's climate built from direct measurements of air and ocean temperatures. From it comes global surface temperature, the mean temperature of Earth's surface at any given time, also called global mean surface temperature (GMST). It blends sea surface temperature with the air temperature just above land, each weighted by how much area it covers. The data come mostly from weather stations and satellites.

paragraphs.heading: How far back it goes
paragraphs.text: Reliable runs of measurements began in some regions between 1850 and 1880. The longest single series, the Central England record, starts in 1659, while the longest records covering most of the globe begin in 1850. Further back, estimates rely on proxy data, drawn for example from tree rings, corals and ice cores. Tree rings and ice cores can give evidence about global temperature over roughly the last 1,000–2,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Above and below the surface
paragraphs.text: Temperatures higher in the atmosphere are measured in other ways, using radiosondes launched on weather balloons, various satellites, and aircraft. Satellites can track the upper air but are not commonly used to measure change at the surface. Ocean temperatures at a range of depths are added to the surface datasets and are also used to work out how much heat the ocean holds.

paragraphs.heading: What the record shows
paragraphs.text: The yearly average GMST rose up to 1940, stayed fairly steady from 1940 to 1975, and has climbed since then by roughly 0.15 °C to 0.20 °C each decade. It now stands at least 1.1 °C above 1880 levels. Comparing 1850–1900 with 2011–2020, several independent datasets show warming of 1.09 °C, within a range of 0.95 to 1.20 °C. The pace since the 1970s is faster than in any other 50-year stretch in at least the last 2000 years. The cooling or plateau between 1940 and 1970 has mostly been put down to sulfate aerosol. Today the yearly average is about 15 °C (59 °F), though single months can sit almost 2 °C above or below it.

paragraphs.heading: Land, sea and cities
paragraphs.text: Air over land is warming faster than the sea surface. From 1850–1900 to 2011–2020, land warmed by 1.59 °C while sea surface temperatures rose 0.88 °C. Within the upward trend, some ups and downs come from natural internal variability, such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation. Uncorrected effects of growing cities or changing land use are unlikely to have raised global land warming by more than 10%. Locally, though, larger city signals have been found in some fast-growing regions such as eastern China.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The rising global surface temperature is one of many lines of evidence behind the scientific consensus that human activities are causing climate change. Temperature changes over the past century show the effects of increasing greenhouse gases, and climate change follows as the climate system responds to them.
